title: The Kojiki — Reading Japan's Oldest Chronicle
description: A close reading of Japan's oldest literary work, the Kojiki (712 CE), in Basil Hall Chamberlain's 1882 translation. Students trace the text's cosmological myths, genealogical arguments, and embedded waka poetry — learning to read the Kojiki not as literal history or simple mythology but as political literature with a complex reception history stretching from Motoori Norinaga's 18th-century commentary to the post-WWII rehabilitation of Japanese scholarship.
learning_outcomes: Explain the Kojiki's political origins and describe the roles of its key compilers
Identify the major deities and trace the genealogical chain from primordial creation to Emperor Jimmu
Read Chamberlain's 1882 translation productively, understanding its strengths and Victorian biases
Analyze key mythological episodes for their political and theological function
Distinguish the waka poems from the surrounding prose and explain what they contribute
Trace the Kojiki's reception history through Norinaga, State Shinto, and post-WWII scholarship
Apply the scholarly concept of 'myth' to explain how ancient narratives function in political and religious contexts
